evidence.quote: The cropping season usually extends from about April to January, with a peak from September to November.
evidence.doc: KwaZulu-Natal Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, 'Fruit and Nut Production in KZN' (Horticultural Advisory Notes), section 1.6 Papaya, 'Bearing age'

harvestMonths.notes: April to January runs across the year end, so February and March are outside the stated season. The same sentence gives a peak of September to November. The paragraph mentions the Makhathini Flats only for how soon the first crop comes, so the season is for KZN in general. The guide has no in-text citation for this sentence (its reference list includes De Villiers 1999, 'The cultivation of Papaya', ARC). Page is the PDF page.

evidence.quote: first crop is generally produced about 18 months later
evidence.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN, Bearing age

yearsToFirstCrop.notes: KZN typical first crop after planting, about 18 months. The same paragraph reports 9–11 months under favourable Makhathini Flats conditions. This is a typical regional reference, not a minimum or guarantee.

yearsToFullBearing.notes: No explicit age of full bearing is sourced. The KZN guide does state an economic plantation life of about 4–5 years; this is retained as a renewal reference rather than incorrectly used as the age of full production.

yieldKgPerTreeMature.notes: Corrected 11 October 2026: KZN DARD supplies conservative 10–15, average 20–25 and good 30 t/ha (PDF p19), plus planting spacing (p18). These regional hectare references are retained below. The guide does not give an annual per-bearing-female yield by age, so arbitrary plant counts, male plants and household spacing cannot receive a generic kg/plant default.

chillUnits.notes: Papaya is a frost-tender tropical/subtropical plant with no winter-chill requirement for flowering, but no fetched source explicitly stated 'no chill requirement' for papaya, so left null per the rule rather than asserting it. The FAO compendium instead notes cold sensitivity in a postharvest-ripening context, not a floral-induction chilling need.

pollination.notes: Set to null in editor review: the FAO quote says papaya plants are male, female or perfect; which applies depends on the cultivar and the plant, so no single value is stated by the source. Withdrawn value: partly-self-fertile.

supplementaryReferences.title: Plantation renewal
supplementaryReferences.quote: The economic life of a plantation is only about 4-5 years.
supplementaryReferences.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Papaya: Bearing age
supplementaryReferences.note: The KZN guide gives about 4–5 years as the economic life of a plantation. Review replanting in the future plan; this commercial renewal reference does not mean every household plant dies at five or starts full production then.

supplementaryReferences.title: Regional hectare output
supplementaryReferences.quote: Yields (t/ha) Conservative: 10 to 15 Average: 20 to 25 Good: 30
supplementaryReferences.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Papaya: Yields
supplementaryReferences.note: Regional production reference: conservative 10–15 t/ha, average 20–25 t/ha, good 30 t/ha. These area figures are not a per-plant annual age schedule. Match plant sex, bearing plants, spacing, climate and water before setting expected kilograms.

supplementaryReferences.title: Starting stock and plant sex
supplementaryReferences.quote: These are solo (or hermaphrodite) varieties eg. ‘Sunrise Solo’, and dioecious (Male and female flowers borne on separate plants) varieties eg. ‘Honey Gold’.
supplementaryReferences.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN (2006), Papaya: Sex forms
supplementaryReferences.note: Sunrise Solo is a hermaphrodite-type candidate; Honey Gold has separate male and female plants. Confirm the actual stock and sex form. A count of mapped plants alone does not establish how many bear fruit.
